**Problem A1: Shake It**
Most hairy mammals shake after getting wet; shaking the water off is energetically advantageous to waiting for it to dry on its own. In this problem, we investigate the mechanics of shaking off water. For simplicity, we will model animals as solid cylinders with the sides covered in fur. You may ignore gravity throughout the problem.

a. We can model the shaking by assuming that the angular position of the cylinder undergoes a sinusoidal oscillation: θ = A cos(ωt). (The rotation is about the axis of rotational symmetry.) Letting the radius of the cylindrical animal be R, derive an expression for the magnitude of the acceleration of a point on the surface of the animal under such a motion.

b. For the rest of this problem, rather than modeling sinusoidal motion, we will assume that the cylindrical animal is simply spinning at constant angular speed ω. Wet fur tends to separate into cylindrical clumps of radius r ≪ R. A droplet of water on the end of a clump of fur will be separated from it if the centripetal force overcomes the forces due to surface tension. Derive an approximate relationship (valid up to scalar numerical constants) between the surface tension σ, the radius r of the fur clump, the radius R of the animal, the angular speed ω, and the density ρ of water. The diagram below show the cross-section of the animal, showing four clumps of fur with droplets on their end.
[Diagram description: A large circle representing the cross-section of the cylindrical animal. On the right side of the circle, four small, closely spaced cylindrical clumps of fur protrude radially outward. Each clump has a small hemispherical droplet of water at its outer end.]

c. Experimentally, it is observed that all mammalian fur forms clumps of similar radius. Under the assumption that different animals all have the same density and are simply scaled copies of each other (i.e. larger animals are both longer and fatter), the relationship between an animal’s mass M and its angular velocity of shaking ω is of the form ω ∼ M^n: find the value of n.

d. Shaking requires energy, which we can crudely model as the rotational energy of the corresponding cylinder. An alternative strategy for the animal is to simply air-dry their fur, which requires energy to evaporate the water. Assume a wet animal has approximately 5% of their body weight in water, and has to supply all the energy for evaporating the water. Our model predicts that for some animal sizes, it will be energetically advantageous to air dry themselves: estimate the range of animal masses for which this is true. You may use the following facts: a mouse weighs 20 g, has a radius of 1 cm, and shakes itself with angular velocity ω = 30 rad/s. The latent heat of vaporization of water at room temperature is λ = 2430 J/g.

**a.  Acceleration of a point on the surface**

For a point at a fixed distance \(R\) from the rotation axis the polar coordinates give  

\[
\mathbf a = -R\,\omega^{2}(t)\,\hat r+R\,\alpha(t)\,\hat\theta ,
\qquad 
\omega(t)=\dot\theta=-A\omega\sin(\omega t),\qquad 
\alpha(t)=\ddot\theta=-A\omega^{2}\cos(\omega t).
\]

Hence the magnitude of the linear acceleration is  

\[
a(t)=\sqrt{\bigl(R\omega^{2}(t)\bigr)^{2}+\bigl(R\alpha(t)\bigr)^{2}}
      =R\omega^{2}\sqrt{A^{2}\cos^{2}\!\omega t+A^{4}\sin^{4}\!\omega t } .
\]

For the small‑amplitude oscillations that are appropriate for animal shaking \((A\ll1)\) the term
\(A^{4}\sin^{4}\!\omega t\) is negligible, giving  

\[
a(t)\simeq R\,A\,\omega^{2}\,|\cos(\omega t)|
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
a_{\max}=R\,A\,\omega^{2}.
\]

So the peak acceleration experienced by a fur‑point is proportional to the product of the
radius, the angular‑amplitude and the square of the shaking frequency.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**b.  Condition for a droplet to be flung off**

A water droplet at the tip of a fur clump can be modelled as a sphere of radius \(r\)
(and volume \(V=\tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}\)).
Its mass is  

\[
m_{\rm drop}= \rho\,V = \frac{4}{3}\pi\rho r^{3}.
\]

When the animal rotates with constant angular speed \(\omega\) the droplet must experience a
centripetal force  

\[
F_{\rm c}= m_{\rm drop}\,R\,\omega^{2}= \frac{4}{3}\pi\rho r^{3}R\,\omega^{2}.
\]

The force that can be retained by surface tension is of order the surface‑tension
force acting around the contact line of the droplet:

\[
F_{\sigma}\sim 2\pi r\,\sigma .
\]

Detachment occurs when \(F_{\rm c}\gtrsim F_{\sigma}\).  Equating the two (up to
order‑unity constants) gives  

\[
\boxed{\;\sigma \;\sim\; \rho\,\omega^{2}\,r^{2}\,R\;}
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\boxed{\;\omega \;\sim\; \sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma}{\rho r^{2}R}}\; } .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**c.  Scaling of shaking frequency with animal size**

All mammalian fur clumps have essentially the same radius \(r\) and the surface tension
\(\sigma\) and water density \(\rho\) are fixed constants.  From the relation above

\[
\omega \propto R^{-1/2}.
\]

For geometrically similar animals the mass scales as the volume, i.e.

\[
M\propto R^{3}\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;R\propto M^{1/3}.
\]

Therefore  

\[
\omega \propto (M^{1/3})^{-1/2}=M^{-1/6}.
\]

Hence the exponent in \(\omega\sim M^{n}\) is  

\[
\boxed{n=-\frac16 } .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**d.  When is it cheaper to let the water evaporate?**

*Energy needed to shake* (treating the animal as a solid cylinder rotating about its axis)

\[
E_{\rm shake}= \frac12 I\omega^{2}
   =\frac12\Bigl(\frac12 MR^{2}\Bigr)\omega^{2}
   =\frac14\,M\,R^{2}\,\omega^{2}.
\]

*Energy needed to evaporate the water* (5 % of the body mass)

\[
E_{\rm evap}= \lambda\,(0.05M),
\qquad \lambda = 2430\;\text{J g}^{-1}=2.43\times10^{6}\;\text{J kg}^{-1}.
\]

Setting the two energies equal gives a condition that is independent of \(M\):

\[
\frac14 R^{2}\omega^{2}=0.05\lambda
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
R^{2}\omega^{2}=0.2\lambda =4.86\times10^{5}\;{\rm m^{2}\,s^{-2}} .
\tag{1}
\]

From part (c) we have the combined scaling  

\[
R^{2}\omega^{2}\;\propto\;M^{1/3}.
\]

Using the mouse data ( \(M_{0}=20\;{\rm g}=0.020\;{\rm kg},\;
R_{0}=1\;{\rm cm}=0.010\;{\rm m},\;
\omega_{0}=30\;{\rm rad\,s^{-1}}\) ) we obtain the proportionality constant

\[
k\equiv\frac{R^{2}\omega^{2}}{M^{1/3}}
   =\frac{(0.01)^{2}(30)^{2}}{(0.020)^{1/3}}
   \approx 0.33\;{\rm m^{2}s^{-2}\,kg^{-1/3}} .
\]

Insert \(k\) into (1):

\[
k\,M_{c}^{1/3}=0.2\lambda
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
M_{c}=\Bigl(\frac{0.2\lambda}{k}\Bigr)^{3}
     \approx\Bigl(\frac{4.86\times10^{5}}{0.33}\Bigr)^{3}
     \approx 3\times10^{18}\ {\rm kg}.
\]

Thus the model predicts that **only for animals heavier than roughly \(10^{18}\) kg** does the
rotational kinetic energy required for shaking exceed the latent‑heat energy needed to
evaporate the water.  The largest real mammals (blue whales, \(M\sim10^{5}\) kg) are many
orders of magnitude lighter; consequently, for every realistic mammal the energetic cost
of shaking is far smaller than the cost of evaporating the water, so shaking is always
the cheaper strategy.

\[
\boxed{\text{Air‑drying becomes advantageous only for }M\gtrsim10^{18}\ {\rm kg}
\;( \text{far beyond any living animal}) } .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Summary**

* **(a)** \(a_{\max}=R\,A\,\omega^{2}\) (for small oscillation amplitude).  
* **(b)** \(\sigma\sim\rho\,\omega^{2}r^{2}R\).  
* **(c)** \(\omega\propto M^{-1/6}\) → exponent \(n=-\tfrac16\).  
* **(d)** Only animals with \(M\gtrsim10^{18}\,\text{kg}\) would find evaporation cheaper; all
real mammals (masses up to \(\sim10^{5}\) kg) are better off shaking.

Problem A2: Black Tides

Consider a spherically symmetric, nonrotating star of mass $m$ and radius $r$. If it gets too close to the supermassive black hole of mass $M \gg m$ at the center of a galaxy, it will be ripped apart by tidal forces. Throughout this problem, neglect relativistic effects and give answers in terms of $G$, $M$, $m$, and $r$. When asked for numbers, assume the star is Sun-like, so that $m = 2 \times 10^{30} \text{ kg}$, $r = 7 \times 10^8 \text{ m}$, and $M = 10^6 m$, and give all numeric answers to one significant figure.

a. Suppose the star orbits the black hole in a circle of radius $R$. What is the radius of curvature of the trajectory of each point on the star's surface? Note that the star does not rotate as it orbits.

b. Gas on the star's surface facing the black hole is attracted to the star by the star's gravity, and pulled away from the star by the black hole's tidal force. Write an expression for the tidal acceleration at the point closest to the black hole.

c. At a radius $R$ where the gravitational and tidal forces are in equilibrium, the star will start being tidally ripped apart. This effect can only be observed when $R$ is outside the black hole's Schwarzschild radius $R_s = 2GM/c^2$. Find an expression for $R$ and numerically evaluate the ratio $R/R_s$.

For the rest of the problem, we consider a star on a parabolic orbit whose periapsis (distance of closest approach) is equal to the radius $R$ found in part c. Near periapsis, the star will be torn apart in a “tidal disruption event”. As a very rough model of this phenomenon, assume the star is initially a single rigid body. The moment it reaches periapsis, it fragments into many rigid pieces which do not interact with other, and feel only the black hole's gravity.

d. Afterward, some of the fragments will escape from the black hole, while the rest remain bound. Numerically evaluate the fraction of the mass which escapes.

e. An escaping fragment has speed $v_f$ when it is far from the black hole. Find the maximum possible value of $v_f$, among all fragments, and evaluate it numerically.

f. A bound fragment orbits with period $T_f$. Find the minimum possible value of $T_f$, among all fragments, and evaluate it numerically.

As bound fragments return to the location of the initial disruption, they collide with other debris, causing them to be absorbed into the black hole's accretion disk. This process produces an enormous amount of light, with the luminosity (or energy emitted over time) proportional to the mass absorption rate. If $t = 0$ at the moment the star fragments apart, then light begins to be emitted at the time you found in part f, and afterward the luminosity scales as $L \propto 1/t^n$ for a constant $n$.

g. Find the value of $n$. Assume for simplicity that the total energies of the bound fragments are uniformly distributed between their minimum and maximum values.
turns.official_answer:
a. $R$
b. $\frac{2GMr}{R^3}$
c. $R = r\left(\frac{2M}{m}\right)^{1/3}$, $R/R_s = 30$
d. $0.5$
e. $v_f = \left(\frac{2M}{m}\right)^{1/6} \sqrt{\frac{Gm}{r}} = 5 \times 10^6 \text{ m/s}$
f. $T_f = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{r^3}{2Gm}} \sqrt{\frac{M}{m}} = 7 \times 10^6 \text{ s} = 80 \text{ days}$
g. $n = 5/3$

**a.  Radius of curvature of a surface point**

The star does not spin, so every point on it has the same velocity and the same centripetal
acceleration as the centre of the star.  
The centre moves on a circle of radius \(R\) with speed \(v=\sqrt{GM/R}\) and acceleration
\(v^{2}/R\) toward the black hole.  
Because the acceleration of any surface point is the same vector, the trajectory of every
point is also a circle of radius \(R\).

\[
\boxed{R_{\rm curvature}=R}
\]

---

**b.  Tidal acceleration at the near side**

The gravitational acceleration of the black hole at a distance \(d\) is \(GM/d^{2}\).
The tidal acceleration across the star is the difference between the acceleration at the
near point \((d=R-r)\) and at the centre \((d=R)\):

\[
a_{\rm tide}= \frac{GM}{(R-r)^{2}}-\frac{GM}{R^{2}}
           \simeq \frac{2GM}{R^{3}}\,r .
\]

(using \((R-r)^{-2}\approx R^{-2}(1+2r/R)\) and keeping the leading term).

\[
\boxed{a_{\rm tide}= \frac{2GM\,r}{R^{3}}}
\]

---

**c.  Tidal‑disruption radius**

The star is ripped apart when the tidal acceleration equals the surface gravity of the
star,
\(g_{\star}=Gm/r^{2}\).  Equating the two forces per unit mass gives  

\[
\frac{2GM\,r}{R^{3}}=\frac{Gm}{r^{2}}
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
R^{3}= \frac{2M}{m}\,r^{3},
\qquad
\boxed{R=r\Bigl(\frac{2M}{m}\Bigr)^{1/3}} .
\]

With the Sun‑like numbers  

\[
\frac{2M}{m}=2\times10^{6},\qquad
\Bigl(2\times10^{6}\Bigr)^{1/3}\simeq 1.26\times10^{2},
\]

\[
R\approx 1.26\times10^{2}\,r
      \approx 1.26\times10^{2}\times7\times10^{8}\ {\rm m}
      \approx 8.8\times10^{10}\ {\rm m}.
\]

The Schwarzschild radius of the black hole is  

\[
R_{s}= \frac{2GM}{c^{2}}
      =\frac{2(6.67\times10^{-11})(2\times10^{36})}{(3.0\times10^{8})^{2}}
      \approx 3.0\times10^{9}\ {\rm m}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\boxed{\frac{R}{R_{s}}\approx\frac{8.8\times10^{10}}{3.0\times10^{9}}\simeq 30 } .
\]

---

**d.  Mass fraction that escapes**

At the instant of fragmentation the centre of the star moves with the parabolic speed  

\[
v_{\rm c}=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}} .
\]

A fragment that is at a distance \(d\) from the black hole at that moment has specific
orbital energy  

\[
\varepsilon(d)=\frac{v_{\rm c}^{2}}{2}-\frac{GM}{d}
               = \frac{GM}{R}-\frac{GM}{d}
               =GM\Bigl(\frac1R-\frac1d\Bigr).
\]

If \(d>R\) the energy is positive → the fragment is unbound (escapes);  
if \(d<R\) the energy is negative → it remains bound.  
The surface that separates the two cases (\(d=R\)) cuts the star into two equal halves,
so exactly one‑half of the mass escapes.

\[
\boxed{\text{escape fraction}= \tfrac12 } .
\]

---

**e.  Maximum asymptotic speed of an escaping fragment**

The fastest escaping fragment is the one that was farthest from the black hole at periapsis,
\(d_{\max}=R+r\).  Its positive energy is  

\[
\varepsilon_{\max}=GM\Bigl(\frac1R-\frac1{R+r}\Bigr)
                 =\frac{GM\,r}{R(R+r)} .
\]

The asymptotic speed follows from \(\tfrac12 v_{f}^{2}= \varepsilon_{\max}\):

\[
v_{f,\max}= \sqrt{\frac{2GM\,r}{R(R+r)}}
          \approx \sqrt{\frac{2GM\,r}{R^{2}}}
          \;\;(\text{since }r\ll R).
\]

Putting the numbers  

\[
v_{f,\max}\approx\sqrt{\frac{2(6.67\times10^{-11})(2\times10^{36})(7\times10^{8})}
                         {(8.8\times10^{10})^{2}}}
            \approx 5\times10^{6}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}} .
\]

\[
\boxed{v_{f,\max}\;\approx\;5\times10^{6}\ {\rm m/s}} .
\]

---

**f.  Minimum orbital period of a bound fragment**

The most tightly bound fragment is the one that was nearest the black hole,
\(d_{\min}=R-r\).  Its specific energy is  

\[
\varepsilon_{\min}=GM\Bigl(\frac1R-\frac1{R-r}\Bigr)
                 =-\frac{GM\,r}{R(R-r)} .
\]

For a bound orbit \(\varepsilon=-GM/(2a)\), so its semi‑major axis is  

\[
a_{\min}= -\frac{GM}{2\varepsilon_{\min}}
        =\frac{R(R-r)}{2r}
        \approx\frac{R^{2}}{2r}
        \approx 5.5\times10^{12}\ {\rm m}.
\]

The orbital period follows Kepler’s third law,
\(T=2\pi\sqrt{a^{3}/(GM)}\):

\[
T_{\min}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{a_{\min}^{3}}{GM}}
        \approx 7.0\times10^{6}\ {\rm s}
        \approx 8\times10^{1}\ {\rm days}.
\]

\[
\boxed{T_{f,\min}\approx 7\times10^{6}\ {\rm s}\;\;( \sim 80\ {\rm days}) } .
\]

---

**g.  Power‑law index of the luminosity decay**

Assume the bound fragments have specific energies uniformly distributed between the most
bound value \(\varepsilon_{\min}\) and zero (the marginally bound case).  
With \(\varepsilon=-GM/(2a)\) and \(T=2\pi\sqrt{a^{3}/(GM)}\) one finds

\[
\varepsilon \propto T^{-2/3}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{d\varepsilon}{dT}\propto T^{-5/3}.
\]

Because the number of fragments per unit energy is constant,
the number arriving per unit time at the disruption site is
\(N(T)\propto T^{-5/3}\).  Identifying the arrival time with the orbital period,
\(t=T\), gives the mass‑accretion rate
\(\dot M\propto t^{-5/3}\).  Since the luminosity \(L\) is proportional to the
accretion rate,

\[
\boxed{L\propto t^{-n}\;\;\text{with}\;\; n=\frac{5}{3}\approx1.7 } .
\]

In this problem, we explore some of the design considerations for an electromagnet.

**a.** Consider an electromagnet consisting of a long solenoid, i.e. a spiral of thin wire wrapped in a single layer around a cylindrical nonmagnetic core. The wire is wrapped in such a way that the adjacent coils almost touch. When a current is sent through the wire, a magnetic field is generated inside the solenoid; this magnetic field exerts an outward force on the wire. Find the pressure $P$ on the solenoid in terms of the magnetic field $B$ inside the solenoid.

**b.** The pressure on the "walls" of the solenoid is counteracted by tension inside the wire. Derive an expression for the maximal achievable magnetic field $B$ in terms of coil radius $a$, wire diameter (thickness) $t \ll a$, and wire tensile strength $\sigma$. (The tensile strength of a material is the force per unit cross-sectional area that needs to be applied in order to pull the material apart.) Assume the wire is circular in cross-section.

**c.** Let $a = 0.1\text{ m}$, $t = 0.001\text{ m}$. The tensile strength of copper is $\sigma = 250\text{ MPa}$, and the permeability of free space is $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ H/m}$. What is the maximum magnetic field that can be achieved in a single-layer solenoid made out of such a wire without the wire snapping?

**d.** In theory, we could generate a stronger field by increasing the wire thickness, but the nonuniform distribution of current inside the wire makes this difficult to analyze.
Instead, consider wrapping the solenoid in many layers of wire. We will place adjacent layers a distance $t$ apart so that they just barely don't touch, and will adjust the current through each wire to equalize the tensile stress. The wire coils span the space from an inner core radius of $a$ to an outer radius of $b$. Estimate the maximum achievable field strength inside this electromagnet. **Electromagnet – maximum magnetic field set by the tensile strength of the windings**  

We treat the solenoid as a long cylinder of radius \(a\) (single‑layer case) or as a hollow cylinder with inner radius \(a\) and outer radius \(b\) (multi‑layer case).  The magnetic field inside a long solenoid is axial and (to an excellent approximation) uniform; the magnetic pressure that pushes outward on the windings is  

\[
P=\frac{B^{2}}{2\mu_{0}} .
\tag{1}
\]

The windings act like a thin cylindrical shell.  For a thin shell of radius \(r\) and wall thickness \(t\) the hoop (tensile) stress produced by an internal pressure \(P\) is  

\[
\sigma_{\theta}= \frac{P\,r}{t}\; .
\tag{2}
\]

The wire can sustain a tensile stress no larger than its tensile strength \(\sigma\).  By setting \(\sigma_{\theta}=\sigma\) we obtain the largest pressure the coil can stand and, via (1), the largest magnetic field.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### a.  Magnetic pressure on the solenoid

From (1) the pressure exerted on the “walls’’ of the solenoid is  

\[
\boxed{P=\dfrac{B^{2}}{2\mu_{0}} } .
\]

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### b.  Single‑layer coil – maximum field

For a single layer wound on a core of radius \(a\) we set \(r=a\) and \(t\) equal to the wire diameter in (2):

\[
\sigma = \frac{P_{\max}\,a}{t}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
P_{\max}= \frac{\sigma\,t}{a}.
\]

Insert this into (1):

\[
\boxed{B_{\max}= \sqrt{\frac{2\mu_{0}\sigma t}{a}} } .
\tag{3}
\]

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### c.  Numerical value for a typical copper coil  

\[
\begin{aligned}
a &=0.10\;\text{m}, &
t &=1.0\times10^{-3}\;\text{m}, &
\sigma &=250\;\text{MPa}=2.5\times10^{8}\;\text{Pa},\\
\mu_{0}&=4\pi\times10^{-7}\;\text{H m}^{-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
B_{\max}&=\sqrt{\frac{2(4\pi\times10^{-7})(2.5\times10^{8})(10^{-3})}{0.10}}\\
&\approx\sqrt{6.28}\;\text{T}\;\approx\;2.5\;\text{T}.
\end{aligned}
\]

\[
\boxed{B_{\max}\approx 2.5\;\text{T}} .
\]

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### d.  Multi‑layer coil (inner radius \(a\), outer radius \(b\))

Now the winding is a **thick‑walled cylinder** with inner radius \(a\) and outer radius \(b\).  
For a thick cylinder with internal pressure \(P\) (the magnetic pressure) the maximum hoop stress occurs at the inner surface:

\[
\sigma_{\max}= \frac{P\,(a^{2}+b^{2})}{b^{2}-a^{2}} .
\tag{4}
\]

Setting \(\sigma_{\max}=\sigma\) and solving for \(P_{\max}\),

\[
P_{\max}= \sigma\,\frac{b^{2}-a^{2}}{a^{2}+b^{2}} .
\tag{5}
\]

The corresponding magnetic field is obtained from (1):

\[
\boxed{B_{\max}= \sqrt{2\mu_{0}\,\sigma\;\frac{b^{2}-a^{2}}{a^{2}+b^{2}}}\; } .
\tag{6}
\]

*Special case:* when the coil is much thicker than its inner radius (\(b\gg a\)), the geometric factor tends to 1 and (6) reduces to the **material limit**

\[
B_{\max}\;\approx\;\sqrt{2\mu_{0}\sigma}.
\tag{7}
\]

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### e.  Numerical value for the given geometry  

\[
a=0.10\;\text{m},\qquad b=0.30\;\text{m},\qquad 
\sigma=2.5\times10^{8}\;\text{Pa},\qquad 
\mu_{0}=4\pi\times10^{-7}\;\text{H m}^{-1}.
\]

The geometric factor is  

\[
\frac{b^{2}-a^{2}}{a^{2}+b^{2}}=
\frac{0.30^{2}-0.10^{2}}{0.10^{2}+0.30^{2}}
=\frac{0.09-0.01}{0.01+0.09}=0.80 .
\]

Insert into (6):

\[
\begin{aligned}
B_{\max}&=
\sqrt{\,2(4\pi\times10^{-7})(2.5\times10^{8})\,(0.80)}\\[2mm]
&=\sqrt{5.0\times10^{2}}\;\text{T}
\;\approx\;2.2\times10^{1}\;\text{T}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Rounded to one significant figure:

\[
\boxed{B_{\max}\approx 2\times10^{1}\ \text{T (≈ 20 T)}} .
\]

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### Summary of results  

| Part | Result |
|------|--------|
| **a** | \(P = B^{2}/(2\mu_{0})\) |
| **b** | \(B_{\max}= \sqrt{2\mu_{0}\sigma t/a}\) |
| **c** | \(B_{\max}\approx 2.5\ \text{T}\) |
| **d** | \(B_{\max}= \sqrt{2\mu_{0}\sigma\,(b^{2}-a^{2})/(a^{2}+b^{2})}\) |
| **e** | \(B_{\max}\approx 2\times10^{1}\ \text{T}\) (≈ 20 T) |

These expressions give the maximum magnetic field that can be generated by a copper‑wire solenoid before the windings fail by tensile yielding.  (Heating, eddy currents, and other practical limitations are ignored in this idealised estimate.)

Consider a disk with mass $m$ and radius $R$ placed on a large and frictionless table. An ant with mass $m$ is placed on top of the disk. The ant can move freely without sliding on the disk.

**Setup**

The disk has mass \(m\) and radius \(R\) (moment of inertia \(I=\tfrac12mR^{2}\)).  
The table is frictionless, so the centre of mass (CM) of the whole system does not move and the total angular momentum about any point is conserved.  
All motion is planar; we use the \(z\)‑axis out of the page.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### a.  Ant walking across a diameter

The ant walks along a diameter with speed \(v\) **relative to the disk**.  
Because the total momentum of the system is zero, the disk moves so that the CM stays fixed.  
If the disk’s centre moves with velocity \(\mathbf V\), the ant’s velocity in the lab is  

\[
\mathbf v_{a}= \mathbf V + \mathbf v_{\rm rel},
\qquad |\mathbf v_{\rm rel}|=v .
\]

Momentum conservation gives \(m\mathbf v_{a}+m\mathbf V=0\;\Rightarrow\;\mathbf V=-\mathbf v_{a}\).  
Substituting,

\[
\mathbf v_{a}= -\mathbf v_{a}+ \mathbf v_{\rm rel}
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\mathbf v_{a}= \frac{\mathbf v_{\rm rel}}{2}.
\]

Hence the ant’s speed in the table frame is  

\[
\boxed{v_{a}= \frac{v}{2}}
\]

directed **toward the opposite edge** (the same direction in which it walks relative to the disk).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### b.  Ant walking around the rim

Now the ant walks counter‑clockwise around the rim with speed \(v\) relative to the disk.  
Let the disk rotate with angular velocity \(\omega\) (positive counter‑clockwise) and translate with velocity \(\mathbf V\).

The ant’s absolute velocity is  

\[
\mathbf v_{a}= \mathbf V + \omega R\,\hat\theta + v\,\hat\theta
            = \mathbf V + (\omega R+v)\,\hat\theta .
\]

The CM stays at rest, so \(m\mathbf v_{a}+m\mathbf V=0\;\Rightarrow\;\mathbf V=-\mathbf v_{a}\).  
Using angular‑momentum conservation (the initial angular momentum is zero) one finds  

\[
\omega = -\frac{v}{2R}.
\]

Thus the absolute speed of the ant is  

\[
|\mathbf v_{a}| = \frac{v}{4}.
\]

The direction is still counter‑clockwise (the disk rotates clockwise, but the ant’s net motion is counter‑clockwise).  

\[
\boxed{v_{a}= \frac{v}{4}\ \text{(counter‑clockwise)}} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### c.  Two ants: when is the inner ant stationary?

Add a second ant of mass \(m\) on a circle of radius \(R/2\).  
The first ant (on the rim) continues to walk around the edge at speed \(v\) (counter‑clockwise) as in part b.  
The second ant walks on its inner circle at speed \(v/2\) (counter‑clockwise) **relative to the disk**.

Because the two walking speeds give the same *relative angular speed* \(\omega_{\rm rel}=v/R\) about the disk centre, the line joining the disk centre to each ant rotates with the same absolute angular speed  

\[
\Omega = \omega+\omega_{\rm rel}.
\]

Write the unit vectors tangent to the two circles as \(\hat\theta_{1}\) and \(\hat\theta_{2}\); the angle between them is the constant offset \(\theta\).

The CM condition gives the velocity of the disk centre:

\[
\mathbf V = -\frac{R\Omega}{3}\,\hat\theta_{1}-\frac{R\Omega}{6}\,\hat\theta_{2}.
\]

The absolute velocity of the inner ant is

\[
\mathbf v_{2}= \mathbf V + \frac{R}{2}\,\Omega\,\hat\theta_{2}
            = \frac{R\Omega}{3}\bigl(\hat\theta_{2}-\hat\theta_{1}\bigr).
\]

For the inner ant to be **stationary in the lab** we need \(\mathbf v_{2}=0\), i.e.

\[
\hat\theta_{2}=\hat\theta_{1}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\theta=0\ (\text{mod }2\pi).
\]

Thus the second ant must lie on the **same radial line** as the first ant (the two ants are aligned).  

\[
\boxed{\theta = 0\ \text{(mod }2\pi\text{)}} .
\]

*(If the first ant were fixed to the rim instead of walking, the same analysis would give \(\theta=\pi\).  In the present problem the first ant is walking as in part b, so the correct answer is \(\theta=0\).)*

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Answers**

* **a.** Ant’s speed in the table frame: \(v/2\) toward the opposite edge.  
* **b.** Ant’s speed in the table frame: \(v/4\) (counter‑clockwise).  
* **c.** The second ant is stationary only when it is aligned with the first ant: \(\displaystyle \theta = 0\ (\text{mod }2\pi)\).

A plane is flying horizontally at constant velocity $v$ and altitude $z = H$. The speed of sound at altitude $z$ is given by
$$c(z) = \alpha \sqrt{T(z)},$$
where $\alpha$ is a constant. Suppose $v > c(H)$, and define the Mach number as
$$M \equiv \frac{v}{c(H)} > 1.$$
If $c(z)$ is constant for all $z$, then the envelope is a cone with half angle $\theta$ where $\sin \theta = \frac{1}{M}$ and propagates with the speed of sound $c$.

a. Sketch the envelope.

b. Now, the speed of sound depends on the altitude because the temperature is not uniform. For the altitudes we are interested in, the following linear model works well:
$$T(z) = T_0 - \beta z,$$
where $\beta > 0$ is a constant. Sketch the envelope of the boom.

c. If the Mach number is large enough then the sonic boom hits the ground. Assume it is large enough. On the ground, there are two sensors at $z = 0$ and $z = h$, one directly above the other. Assume $h \ll H$ and $\beta h \ll T_0$. At time $t_1$, the top sensor receives the sonic boom signal and at a later time, the bottom sensor also receives the signal. Express the Mach number $M$ of the airplane in terms of $H, h, t, T_0, \alpha, \beta$, where $t = t_2 - t_1$.

d. If the plane travels slower without changing direction, its sonic boom could become no longer audible from the ground for the Mach number $1 < M < M_{\text{max}}$. What is the upper limit for the Mach number $M_{\text{max}}$ for which this can occur? Express your answer in terms of $T_0, H, \alpha, \beta$. You do not necessarily need all of these parameters.

turns.candidate_answer:
**Problem B2 – “Where’s the Kaboom?”**

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### a.  Envelope for a uniform atmosphere  

When the speed of sound is the same at every altitude the plane’s Mach cone is a straight cone.  
With the plane moving horizontally at speed \(v\) the Mach angle \(\mu\) satisfies  

\[
\sin\mu=\frac{c}{v}=\frac{1}{M},
\qquad M\equiv\frac{v}{c(H)}>1 .
\]

The Mach front is a line that makes an angle \(\mu\) with the direction of flight (the
horizontal).  It leaves the plane at the altitude \(z=H\) and meets the ground at a
horizontal distance  

\[
X_{\rm g}=H\cot\mu=\frac{H}{\tan\mu}
      =H\frac{\sqrt{M^{2}-1}}{1}\; .
\]

*Sketch:* a right‑triangle whose hypotenuse is the Mach line, the vertical side is the
altitude \(H\) and the horizontal side is \(X_{\rm g}\).  The cone is a straight
double‑cone symmetric about the flight path.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### b.  Envelope when the speed of sound varies with altitude  

Now \(c(z)=\alpha\sqrt{T(z)}=\alpha\sqrt{T_{0}-\beta z}\) ( \(\beta>0\) so the air is colder
near the ground).  At the altitude of the plane

\[
\sin\mu(H)=\frac{c(H)}{v}=\frac{1}{M},
\]

so the Mach line leaves the plane with the same initial angle as in the uniform case.
Because the sound speed decreases as the wave descends, Snell’s law for a stratified
medium gives a constant horizontal slowness  

\[
\frac{\sin\theta(z)}{c(z)}=\frac{1}{v}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\sin\theta(z)=\frac{c(z)}{v}\; .
\]

Hence the ray (the normal to the Mach front) becomes **more horizontal** as \(z\) decreases:
\(\theta(z)\) decreases because \(c(z)\) decreases.  The Mach line therefore bends
downward, becoming shallower as it approaches the ground.

*Sketch:* a curve that starts from the plane with the same angle \(\mu(H)\) as in part (a)
but gradually flattens, meeting the ground at a larger horizontal distance than the
uniform‑\(c\) case.  The curve is concave upward (the curvature is larger near the
ground because \(c\) is lower there).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### c.  Mach number from the arrival‑time difference of two nearby sensors  

Two sensors are placed at \(z=0\) (ground) and at a small height \(z=h\) (\(h\ll H\) and
\(\beta h\ll T_{0}\)).  The upper sensor receives the boom at time \(t_{1}\) and the lower
sensor at a later time \(t_{2}=t_{1}+t\); we are asked for \(M\) in terms of the given
quantities.

The normal to the Mach front travels with speed \(c(z)\) and makes an angle
\(\theta(z)\) to the horizontal.  Its **vertical component** is

\[
v_{z}(z)=c(z)\sin\theta(z)=c(z)\,\frac{c(z)}{v}
        =\frac{c^{2}(z)}{v}\; .
\]

Thus a vertical element \(dz\) is traversed in a time  

\[
dt = \frac{dz}{v_{z}(z)} = \frac{v\,dz}{c^{2}(z)} .
\]

Integrating from the ground to the upper sensor gives the measured time difference

\[
t = \int_{0}^{h}\frac{v\,dz}{c^{2}(z)}
   \;\approx\; \frac{v\,h}{c^{2}(0)}\;,
\qquad\bigl(\beta h\ll T_{0}\bigr) .
\]

Here \(c(0)=\alpha\sqrt{T_{0}}\) and \(v=M\,c(H)=M\,\alpha\sqrt{T_{0}-\beta H}\).
Solving for \(M\),

\[
\boxed{ \displaystyle
M = \frac{c^{2}(0)}{c(H)}\;\frac{t}{h}
   = \frac{\alpha^{2}T_{0}}{\alpha\sqrt{T_{0}-\beta H}}\;\frac{t}{h}
   = \frac{\alpha\,T_{0}}{h\sqrt{T_{0}-\beta H}}\;t } .
\]

Equivalently, in terms of the speeds of sound at the two altitudes,

\[
\boxed{ M = \frac{c^{2}(0)}{c(H)}\;\frac{t}{h}
      =\frac{c(0)^{2}\,t}{c(H)\,h}} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### d.  Upper limit of Mach number for which the boom can become inaudible  

The Mach front can reach the ground only if the plane’s speed exceeds the local sound
speed at ground level.  The condition for a ground‑observable boom is therefore  

\[
v > c(0) .
\]

Since \(v = M\,c(H)\),

\[
M\,c(H) > c(0)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
M > \frac{c(0)}{c(H)}
   = \frac{\alpha\sqrt{T_{0}}}{\alpha\sqrt{T_{0}-\beta H}}
   = \sqrt{\frac{T_{0}}{T_{0}-\beta H}} .
\]

If \(M\) is **greater** than this ratio the boom will always be heard on the ground,
even after a small reduction in speed.  If \(M\) lies between the sonic threshold
\(1\) and this value, slowing the plane can make the boom disappear (the Mach front
stops above the ground).  Hence the largest Mach number for which the boom can become
inaudible is

\[
\boxed{ \displaystyle
M_{\max}= \sqrt{\frac{T_{0}}{\,T_{0}-\beta H\,}} } .
\]

(Only the atmospheric temperature profile is needed; the constant \(\alpha\) cancels.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Summary of results**

| Part | Result |
|------|--------|
| **a** | Straight Mach cone with half‑angle \(\mu\) given by \(\sin\mu=1/M\). |
| **b** | Curved Mach front, initially inclined at \(\mu(H)=\arcsin(c(H)/v)\), bending to a shallower angle as it descends because \(c(z)\) decreases. |
| **c** | \( \displaystyle M = \frac{\alpha\,T_{0}}{h\sqrt{T_{0}-\beta H}}\;t \) |
| **d** | \( \displaystyle M_{\max}= \sqrt{\frac{T_{0}}{T_{0}-\beta H}} \) |

These expressions give the required Mach‑number dependence on the atmospheric
temperature gradient and the geometry of the sonic‑boom envelope.

**Problem B3: Locked and Moded**

a. Consider two mirrors facing each other separated by a distance $L$ (a Fabry–Pérot resonator). The cavity (the space between the two mirrors) is in vacuum (index of refraction $n = 1$, no dispersion), and the mirrors have high reflectivities so that the main resonance condition is that an integer multiple of half-wavelengths fit into the cavity. A light pulse containing multiple different frequencies travels between the mirrors and interferes with itself.
i. State the condition for resonance in terms of $L$ and wavelength $\lambda$.
ii. Write down an expression for the resonant angular frequencies $\omega_m$, with $m$ counting each of the possible resonances.
iii. What is the angular frequency spacing $\Delta\omega \equiv \omega_{m+1} - \omega_m$ between adjacent angular frequencies?

b. The electric field at the antinodes of the standing waves in the resonator is a superposition of oscillations at the resonant angular frequencies and is given by:
$$E_{\text{before}}(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{+\infty} E_k \cos[(k \Delta\omega) t]$$
Now suppose we introduce a gain medium (such as a doped crystal) into the laser cavity. The gain medium completely absorbs incoming light and re-emits it over a finite range of $N$ angular frequencies centered around some angular frequency $\omega_0$, which coincides with one of the $\omega_m$ values determined above. Within this bandwidth, the gain medium amplifies and supports oscillations at all $\omega_m$ that fall within the range. (Assume $N$ is an odd number.)
Assume that each of these $N$ angular frequencies—also referred to as modes—has the same amplitude $E_0$, and that their phases are locked such that there is zero relative phase between them at $t = 0$. This condition is known as mode locking. Set their common phase so that all electric fields are expressed as cosine functions, consistent with the form of $E_{\text{before}}(t)$.
i. Write an expression for the total electric field $E_{\text{after}}(t)$ as the sum of these $N$ equally spaced angular frequencies (with zero relative phase).
ii. Show that in the limit of many angular frequencies ($\Delta\omega \ll \omega_0$, $N \gg 1$), the time-dependent electric field approximately takes the following form:
$$E_{\text{after}}(t) \approx E_0 f(\omega_0, t) \frac{\sin\left(\frac{N (\Delta\omega) t}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{(\Delta\omega) t}{2}\right)}$$
and determine the function $f(\omega_0, t)$.

c. To answer the next part of the problem, assume $N$ is odd and find the following limit when $a = \pi m$, where $m$ is an integer:
$$\lim_{x \to a} \frac{\sin(Nx)}{\sin x}$$

d. Mode locking can dramatically increase the peak intensity $I$ of the laser output. Use the expression $I = \gamma E^2$, where $\gamma$ is a known constant, to answer the following questions.
i. Determine the total instantaneous intensity $I_{\text{after}}(t)$ of the electric field.
ii. What is the maximum possible intensity of the total field, and at what time(s) is this achieved?

e. The uncertainty principle states $\Delta x \Delta p \ge \frac{\hbar}{2}$. In optics, we are more commonly interested in the duration of the pulse rather than its spatial extent; the two are related via $\Delta x = c \Delta t$. Consider the problem of setting up a very short laser pulse. Use the uncertainty principle to estimate the required bandwidth (range of frequencies). Compare that to the relationship between pulse duration and gain bandwidth that we're achieving in this problem.

**Problem B3 – “Locked and Moded’’**

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### a.   Resonance of a Fabry–Pérot cavity  

1. **Resonance condition** – an integer number of half‑wavelengths must fit into the cavity  

\[
\boxed{2L=m\lambda\qquad\bigl(m=1,2,3,\dots\bigr)}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
L=\frac{m\lambda}{2}.
\]

2. **Resonant angular frequencies** – using \(\omega =2\pi c/\lambda\)

\[
\boxed{\omega_m = \frac{2\pi c}{\lambda_m}= \frac{2\pi c}{2L/m}= \frac{m\pi c}{L}},\qquad
m=0,\pm1,\pm2,\dots
\]

(Any integer index may be chosen; the spacing does not depend on the sign.)

3. **Frequency spacing**

\[
\boxed{\Delta\omega\equiv\omega_{m+1}-\omega_m=\frac{\pi c}{L}} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### b.   Mode‑locked field after the gain medium  

Let the gain bandwidth contain \(N\) equally spaced modes \((N\;{\rm odd})\) centred on
\(\omega_0\) (one of the \(\omega_m\)).  The modes have the same amplitude \(E_0\) and are
phase‑locked with zero relative phase at \(t=0\).

---

#### i.   Exact sum

Choose the symmetric index set  
\(k=-(N-1)/2,\dots,+(N-1)/2\).  Then

\[
\boxed{E_{\rm after}(t)=
\sum_{k=-(N-1)/2}^{+(N-1)/2}E_0\cos\!\bigl[(\omega_0+k\Delta\omega)\,t\bigr]} .
\]

---

#### ii.   Form in the limit \(N\gg1,\;\Delta\omega\ll\omega_0\)

Use the identity for a finite sum of cosines

\[
\sum_{k=-(N-1)/2}^{+(N-1)/2}\!\cos(\alpha+k\beta)
   =\cos\alpha\;\frac{\sin(N\beta/2)}{\sin(\beta/2)} ,
\]

with \(\alpha=\omega_0 t\) and \(\beta=\Delta\omega\,t\).  Hence

\[
\boxed{E_{\rm after}(t)\;\approx\;E_0\,
\cos(\omega_0t)\,
\frac{\sin\!\bigl(N\Delta\omega\,t/2\bigr)}
     {\sin\!\bigl(\Delta\omega\,t/2\bigr)} } .
\]

Thus  

\[
\boxed{f(\omega_0,t)=\cos(\omega_0t)} .
\]

The first factor \(\cos(\omega_0t)\) is the optical carrier, the fraction of sines is the
slowly‑varying envelope.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### c.   Limit of \(\displaystyle \frac{\sin(Nx)}{\sin x}\) as \(x\to a=\pi m\)

For integer \(m\) and odd \(N\),

\[
\lim_{x\to\pi m}\frac{\sin(Nx)}{\sin x}
   =\lim_{x\to\pi m}\frac{N\cos(Nx)}{\cos x}
   =N\,\frac{(-1)^{Nm}}{(-1)^{m}}
   =N,
\]

because \(N-1\) is even, making \((-1)^{(N-1)m}=1\).

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}\frac{\sin(Nx)}{\sin x}=N } .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### d.   Intensity of the mode‑locked pulse  

The instantaneous intensity is \(I(t)=\gamma E^{2}(t)\).

---

#### i.   Instantaneous intensity

\[
\boxed{
I_{\rm after}(t)=\gamma\,E_{0}^{2}\,
\cos^{2}(\omega_0t)\,
\left[\frac{\sin\!\bigl(N\Delta\omega\,t/2\bigr)}
          {\sin\!\bigl(\Delta\omega\,t/2\bigr)}\right]^{2}
}.
\]

---

#### ii.   Maximum intensity and when it occurs  

The envelope factor attains its **global maximum** when the ratio
\(\displaystyle\frac{\sin(N\Delta\omega t/2)}{\sin(\Delta\omega t/2)}\) tends to \(N\).
From part (c) this happens at the instants  

\[
\Delta\omega\,t/2 = p\pi\quad(p=0,\pm1,\pm2,\dots),
\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad
t=\frac{2\pi p}{\Delta\omega},
\]

where the carrier also satisfies \(\cos(\omega_0t)=\pm1\).  At those times the envelope
value is \(N\) and the carrier is at a peak, so

\[
\boxed{I_{\max}= \gamma\,E_{0}^{2}\,N^{2}
       = N^{2}\,I_{0}},
\]

where \(I_{0}=\gamma E_{0}^{2}\) is the intensity of a single mode.  
The maximum is achieved whenever

\[
t =\frac{2\pi p}{\Delta\omega}\quad\text{and}\quad
\omega_0 t = q\pi\;(q\in\mathbb Z),
\]

i.e. when the pulse repetition period (set by the cavity) and the optical‑carrier
phase both line up.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### e.   Bandwidth–duration relation from the uncertainty principle  

The uncertainty principle for a photon packet,
\(\Delta x\,\Delta p \ge \hbar/2\), together with \(\Delta x = c\Delta t\) and
\(\Delta p = \hbar\,\Delta k = \hbar\,\Delta\omega /c\), gives

\[
c\Delta t\;\frac{\hbar\Delta\omega}{c}\;\gtrsim\;\frac{\hbar}{2}
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\boxed{\Delta\omega\,\Delta t\;\gtrsim\;\frac12}\;\;( \approx 1\; \text{to order of magnitude}).
\]

Thus a pulse of duration \(\Delta t\) requires a **frequency bandwidth** of order

\[
\Delta\omega \;\sim\;\frac{1}{\Delta t}
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\Delta\nu \;\sim\;\frac{1}{2\pi\Delta t}.
\]

In a mode‑locked laser the total gain bandwidth is the span covered by the \(N\) locked
modes:

\[
\Delta\omega_{\rm tot}=N\Delta\omega .
\]

The pulse width (full‑width at half‑maximum of the intensity envelope) is essentially the
inverse of this total bandwidth:

\[
\Delta t_{\rm pulse}\;\approx\;\frac{1}{N\Delta\omega}
   =\frac{1}{\Delta\omega_{\rm tot}} .
\]

Hence the mode‑locked system obeys exactly the same bandwidth‑duration scaling demanded
by the uncertainty principle.  Adding more modes (increasing \(N\)) widens the total
gain bandwidth and therefore shortens the pulse, illustrating how mode‑locking is a
practical way to generate pulses whose duration is limited only by the uncertainty
principle.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Answer Summary**

| Part | Result |
|------|--------|
| **a.i** | \(2L=m\lambda\) |
| **a.ii** | \(\displaystyle\omega_m=\frac{m\pi c}{L}\) |
| **a.iii** | \(\displaystyle\Delta\omega=\frac{\pi c}{L}\) |
| **b.i** | \(\displaystyle E_{\rm after}(t)=\sum_{k=-(N-1)/2}^{+(N-1)/2}E_0\cos[(\omega_0+k\Delta\omega)t]\) |
| **b.ii** | \(\displaystyle E_{\rm after}(t)\approx E_0\cos(\omega_0t)\,\frac{\sin(N\Delta\omega t/2)}{\sin(\Delta\omega t/2)}\) with \(f(\omega_0,t)=\cos(\omega_0t)\) |
| **c** | \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}\frac{\sin(Nx)}{\sin x}=N\) |
| **d.i** | \(\displaystyle I_{\rm after}(t)=\gamma E_0^2\cos^2(\omega_0t)\Bigl[\frac{\sin(N\Delta\omega t/2)}{\sin(\Delta\omega t/2)}\Bigr]^2\) |
| **d.ii** | \(\displaystyle I_{\max}=\gamma E_0^2 N^2\) (attained when \(\Delta\omega t/2=p\pi\) and \(\omega_0t=q\pi\)) |

These results describe the resonance spectrum of a Fabry–Pérot cavity, the formation of a
mode‑locked pulse, its intensity envelope, and the fundamental bandwidth–duration limit
imposed by quantum mechanics.
